Lake Erie was named after the Native Americans who lived along its southern shore when Europeans arrived in the 1600s. The name “Erie” is a shortened form of the Iroquoian word “Erielhonan,” meaning “long tail,” which refers to the Eastern Cougar.

By the 16th century, settlements dotted the shores of Lake Huron. One settlement had more than 100 large structures and a population between 4,000 and 6,000.
At this time, the lake was called Karegnondi by the Wyandot, which translated to "Freshwater Sea" 🧵 4/6

AND ANOTHER THING: Ohio's name originates from the Seneca word "ohi:yo," meaning "beautiful river." Lake Erie, named after the Erie Indians who lived on its southern shores, comes from "erielhonan," an Iroquoian term meaning "long tail."

The Great Lakes had Indigenous names long before colonization. Lake Superior was Gichigami (Ojibwe: "Great sea"), Lake Michigan was Mishi-gami ("Large water"), Lake Huron was Karegnondi ("Freshwater sea"), Lake Erie was Erielhonan ("Long tail"), and Lake Ontario was Ontarí'io ("Shining waters").
